title: The Great Migration
subtitle: The Plot of Dar al-Nadwah, the Sanctuary of Thawr, and the Journey to Freedom
summary: The secret departures of early believers to Yathrib, Quraysh's assassination plot in Dar al-Nadwah, Ali's sacrifice in the Prophet's bed, three days in Cave Thawr with Abu Bakr, divine tranquility in the face of pursuers, and the coastal ride toward destiny.

sections.text: The Silent Exodus to Yathrib

Following the Second Pledge of Aqabah, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ issued permission for his followers to migrate to Yathrib. In small family groups and covert pairs under cover of darkness, the Muslims slipped away from Makkah, abandoning their ancestral estates, businesses, and possessions. Men like Suhayb al-Rumi surrendered their entire hard-earned life savings to Quraysh just to be granted passage, earning the Prophet's praise: 'Suhayb has profited; Suhayb has profited!' Within months, entire quarters of Makkah lay deserted, the silence of their shuttered homes testifying to the believers' unshakeable priority of faith over worldly comfort.

Only three principal figures remained behind in Makkah by divine intention: the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ awaiting specific divine permission to depart, his inseparable companion Abu Bakr al-Siddiq who had prepared two well-fed riding camels for the journey, and his young cousin Ali ibn Abi Talib. In addition, a vulnerable group of indigent and imprisoned believers remained whose families physically barred them from departure.
The arid desert expanse where caravans journeyed between Makkah and Madinah.
The Conspiracy of Dar al-Nadwah

Realizing that an independent Muslim sanctuary had formed in Yathrib along their vital northern trade routes to Syria, the aristocracy of Quraysh gathered in extraordinary assembly at Dar al-Nadwah. Various proposals were debated: some urged imprisoning Muhammad behind iron bars until he perished; others suggested exiling him into the desert. Abu Jahl then put forward a chillingly calculated plan: select a noble youth from each clan, arm them with sharp swords, and have them strike the Prophet simultaneously as one man. In this manner, blood responsibility would be dispersed among all the tribes of Quraysh, leaving Banu Hashim incapable of warring against all clans and forcing them to accept monetary blood money.
This treacherous council is immortalized in Surah Al-Anfal in the Holy Quran:

وَإِذْ يَمْكُرُ بِكَ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا لِيُثْبِتُوكَ أَوْ يَقْتُلُوكَ أَوْ يُخْرِجُوكَ ۚ وَيَمْكُرُونَ وَيَمْكُرُ اللَّهُ ۖ وَاللَّهُ خَيْرُ الْمَاكِرِينَ
'And [remember] when those who disbelieved plotted against you to imprison you or kill you or expel you. But they plan, and God plans, and God is the best of planners.' (Surah Al-Anfal 8:30)
The Night of Departure and Ali's Valor

Forewarned by the Angel Jibril, the Prophet visited Abu Bakr at midday to finalize their travel arrangements. As darkness fell, the armed assassins surrounded the Prophet's modest home, peering through the door fissures and waiting for him to step outside at dawn. The Prophet instructed Ali ibn Abi Talib to wrap himself in his green Hadrami mantle and lie in his bed, assuring him: 'Sleep upon my bed; no harm that you detest will reach you from them.' Ali accepted the perilous assignment with absolute tranquility, willingly offering his life as a shield so that the trusts and financial deposits held by the Prophet for the people of Makkah could be safely returned to their owners.

Under the veil of night, reciting verses from Surah Ya-Sin ('And We have put before them a barrier and behind them a barrier and covered them, so they do not see'), the Prophet walked directly past the encircling sentries. A slumber had fallen upon them; he cast a handful of dust over their heads and departed undetected into the night.
Three Days in the Cave of Thawr

Anticipating that Quraysh would immediately scour the northern route toward Yathrib, the Prophet and Abu Bakr executed a brilliant diversion. They headed south of Makkah, climbing the steep, rocky slopes of Mount Thawr to conceal themselves in a secluded cave near its summit. There they remained for three days and nights, supported by an ingenious, covert logistical network.

Abu Bakr's intelligent son, Abdullah, spent his days mingling with the nobles of Quraysh in Makkah, gathering intelligence and climbing up to the cave under cover of night to brief the travelers. Abu Bakr's courageous daughter, Asma, prepared their provisions, tearing her waist girdle in two to bind the food bag—earning the eternal epithet 'Dhat al-Nitaqayn' (She of the Two Girdles). Abu Bakr's shepherd, Amir ibn Fuhayrah, grazed his flock behind Abdullah to erase all footprints from the rocky paths, also providing fresh milk to the hidden companions.
The rugged heights of Mount Thawr where divine serenity triumphed over tribal pursuit.
Divine Tranquility in the Face of Danger

Furious at the Prophet's escape, Quraysh announced a colossal bounty: one hundred camels for whoever brought Muhammad or Abu Bakr dead or alive. Expert desert trackers followed faint traces all the way to the mouth of the cave. Standing just feet outside the entrance, their voices audible within, Abu Bakr whispered in agony: 'O Messenger of God, if one of them were to look down at his feet, he would surely see us!'
The Prophet replied with serene, unshakeable certainty:

يَا أَبَا بَكْرٍ، مَا ظَنُّكَ بِاثْنَيْنِ اللَّهُ ثَالِثُهُمَا؟
'O Abu Bakr, what think you of two companions when God is their third?' (Sahih al-Bukhari & Sahih Muslim)

This transcendent scene is immortalized in Surah At-Tawbah: 'If you do not aid him, God has already aided him when those who disbelieved had driven him out as one of two, when they were in the cave and he said to his companion: Do not grieve; indeed God is with us' (9:40). Blinded by divine protection, the trackers turned away.

On the fourth day, when the initial search abated, their hired non-Muslim navigator, Abdullah ibn Urayqit, arrived with their two camels. Avoiding conventional highways, he guided them along the desolate coastal route by the Red Sea. When Suraqah ibn Malik pursued them for the bounty, his horse repeatedly sank knee-deep into hard sand until he realized the divine protection guarding the travelers; Suraqah surrendered, asked for pardon, and turned back to mislead other pursuers. The path to Madinah lay open.
